questions.stem:
Statements: P > Q = R ≥ S < T; U ≤ S > W

Conclusions:
I. P > T
II. W < P

Study the statements and decide which conclusions necessarily follow. Use only the stated relationships.
options: If only conclusion I is true
If only conclusion II is true
If either conclusion I or II is true
If neither conclusion I nor II is true
If both conclusions I and II are true
questions.explanation:
Source answer: (b) If only conclusion II is true

Conclusion I (P > T) does not necessarily follow. For example, I = 0, P = 1/2, Q = 0, R = 0, S = 0, T = 1/2, U = 0, W = -1/2 satisfies all the statements but makes this conclusion false.

Conclusion II (W < P) follows: its opposite contradicts the stated relationships.

Therefore: If only conclusion II is true.

questions.stem:
How is Q related to Y?
Study the following information carefully and answer the questions given below:
Q is the only daughter of R who is the mother - in - law of U. S is the paternal grandfather of Q’s nephew. S
has two sons, one daughter and no siblings. X is the sister - in - law of T . U is the mother of Y who is married
male. W is the uncle of T who is not a daughter of V. P is the aunt of V who is sibling of Q and W.
questions.explanation:
Source answer: (b) Aunt

S and R are the parents of sons V and W and daughter Q. V and U are the parents of Y and T; Y is male and T is not a daughter of V, so T is male. X is Y's wife, which makes her T's sister-in-law. P is R's sister (S has no siblings), so W is P's nephew. Q is Y's aunt. Among Y, T, P, W and S, P is the female member and the others are male.

questions.stem:
What will be the code for “smile” as per the given code language?
Answer these questions based on the following information.
In a certain code:
“happy not bad good towards” is coded as - “xa pb ut nq tf”
“good smile sorrow towards” is coded as - “ut tf rd lk”
“smile happy not sad” is coded as - “pb rd xa zh”
“bad sorrow towards” is coded as - “nq lk ut”
questions.explanation:
Source answer: (b) rd

Compare the repeated words across the given sentences. A word and its code occur in the same sentences. This gives:

bad → nq
good → tf
happy → pb or xa
not → pb or xa
sad → zh
smile → rd
sorrow → lk
towards → ut

Where two words share the same possible codes, their individual codes cannot be distinguished without an additional clue. Apply any extra code given in this question before selecting the answer.

questions.stem:
Statements: Only a few apple is orange.
Some orange is grapes.
No grapes are banana.
Conclusions:
I. Some grapes are not apple.
II. All apple being banana is a possibility.
In each of the questions below, some statements are given followed by conclusions/group of
conclusions. You have to assume all the statements to be true even if they seem to be at variance from
the commonly known facts and then decide which of the given co nclusions logically follow from the
information given in the statements:
options: If either conclusion I or II follows
If neither conclusion I nor II follows
If both conclusions I and II follow
questions.explanation:
Source answer: (b) If only conclusion II follows

The orange–grapes overlap need not include an object outside apple, so I is not established. Apples may all be bananas if their orange overlap avoids grapes; no statement rules that arrangement out. Only possibility II follows.

questions.stem:
Statements: All cat are dog.
Some dog are not lion.
Only a few tigers are lion.
Conclusions:
I. All cat being lion is a possibility.
II. All tigers being lion is a possibility.
In each of the questions below, some statements are given followed by conclusions/group of
conclusions. You have to assume all the statements to be true even if they seem to be at variance from
the commonly known facts and then decide which of the given co nclusions logically follow from the
information given in the statements:
options: If either conclusion I or II follows
If neither conclusion I nor II follows
If both conclusions I and II follow
questions.explanation:
Source answer: (a) If only conclusion I follows

Cats can all be placed in the dog–lion overlap without contradicting the existence of other dogs outside lion, so I is possible. "Only a few tigers are lion" explicitly requires some tigers outside lion, making II impossible.

questions.stem:
Statements: Some pen are pencil.

No pen are marker.

I. Some eraser are not marker.
II. Some eraser are marker.
In each of the questions below, some statements are given followed by conclusions/group of
conclusions. You have to assume all the statements to be true even if they seem to be at variance from

If both conclusions I and II follow

Source answer: (a) If only conclusion I follows

"Only pencil are eraser" gives eraser ⊆ pencil. The pen–pencil overlap does not guarantee an eraser–pen overlap, so neither conclusion I nor II is individually established. They are complementary alternatives. The PDF keys only I, which needs an additional intended exclusivity premise.

questions.stem:
180 meters long train A crosses train B having length of 120 meters and running in opposite
direction in 60/11 seconds. If speed of train A is 6/5 th of the speed of train B, then find the time taken by
both trains to cross each other, when they running in same direction?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (a) 60 sec

Combined length = 300 m. Opposite-direction speed sum = 300 ÷ (60/11) = 55 m/s. With speed ratio 6:5, the speed difference is 5 m/s. Same-direction crossing time = 300/5 = 60 seconds.
